author: Walter Isaacson
introFa: کتاب «Steve Jobs (Adapted Biography)» نوشته Walter Isaacson یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Steve Jobs (Adapted Biography)»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Chapter 1 – Charisma “Look at Steve Jobs, someone who was really, really not charismatic originally. He made a conscious decision to learn charisma, to create the Steve Jobs ‘persona.’” – Olivia Fox Cabane, The Economist. One of the keys to Steve Jobs’ success, was the persona that he created. Customers adored him, employees followed him and competitors respected him. The respect that Jobs’ commanded thanks to his charisma, saw a welcome return to Apple, stocks flying after his press releases and falling when he fell ill. Jobs’ persona became the personality of Apple. Innovative, experimental and bold. Everything we associate with Apple today leads back to Jobs’ ability to dominate a boardroom, to silence crowds, to persuade, entertain and excite. Being the public face of a company, charisma is everything. If you don’t think of yourself as a particularly charismatic person, there’s no need to worry. A few, very simple techniques will help you develop your charm and come across as a more charismatic person. The first is presence. Simply put, presence is how engaged you are with those around you. During a board meeting if you spend your time staring out the window and not making any eye contact, your colleagues will assume you are not listening, which I don’t have to tell you isn’t very charismatic at all. Another quick trick to boost your charisma is making full use of your body language. When we watch Jobs in press releases and interviews, he makes full use of his hands whilst he talks. The benefits of this may seem subtle, but when you compare someone with active body language, to someone standing stiff and still, the speaker whom moves is significantly more engaging. Charisma is not about reinventing yourself as someone else. The persona that Steve Jobs put forwards was not an entirely fabricated one. He truly did love music, dress modestly, hate market research

and have a philosophical outlook on life. Most people in the world are the same, especially in hating market research. What Steve Jobs did, was present these qualities of himself to the world in a likable manner. An inspirational everyman. Jobs was unique in being himself, but very relatable. He wasn’t just another chief executive in a suit, he took being a normal human being, and used it to make himself stand out. Most public speakers employ persuasive techniques and various rhetoric to draw in a crowd and project a charismatic nature. Steve Jobs took these persuasive techniques, and developed them further. He mixed various techniques to suit the specific situation in which he found himself. “We found that Jobs did not exhibit a single rhetorical style, but rather altered it depending on the situation and yet still managed to deliver a constant message to support his company’s strategy” – Professor Heracleous, Charismatic Leadership and Rhetorical Competence: An Analysis of Steve Jobs’ Rhetoric. Being adaptable plays a huge part in developing charisma, utilizing the same techniques for a variety of audiences will only make you appear robotic and contrived. Stories and Anecdotes were favorites of Jobs, much preferred to statistics and facts. True stories help build a rapport with the audience and develop pathos, one of Aristotle’s modes of persuasion. By using stories that appeal to the audiences emotions, Jobs plays on empathy. This is a big factor on why he was always seen in a black turtleneck sweatshirt and Levis jeans. It made him more human. Confidence is necessary to charisma. No one’s going to like the kid quietly sitting in the corner, because there’s no reason to. They haven’t done anything memorable or exciting. People love a trendsetter or a rebel. These personas thrive on confidence. Steve Jobs famously hated market research, stating that: “You can't just ask customers what they want then try to give that to them. By the time

you get it built, they'll want something new." And for this reason Jobs did what he wanted, made products for himself. The confidence he used to break away from the mold and follow his instincts lead to massive success. Famously, Jobs used his ethos or his credibility to convince and persuade, but when that wasn’t sufficient, Jobs would appeal to the audience’s emotion, or use logic (logos) to carry a point across. With command over Aristotle’s modes of persuasion (ethos, pathos and logos), and confidence to break away from the mold letting your own personality shine through, you can demand respect and authority no matter who you are talking to. Employees, customers and investors will hang on your every word if they can relate to you, as well as be persuaded.

Chapter 2 – Management skills “My model for business is The Beatles. They were four guys who kept each other’s kind of negative tendencies in check. They balanced each other and the total was greater than the sum of the parts. That’s how I see business: great things in business are never done by one person, they’re done by a team of people.” – Steve Jobs. Charisma is necessary when building a team. Charisma will lead to respect. If your employees and colleagues respect you, then your ability to push and inspire them to new heights is drastically increased. The success of any business relies on the competencies of its employees. All supervisors, managers and executives are responsible for the quality of work produced by those they oversee. Your charisma and the respect that you have earned through techniques we mentioned earlier (ethos, pathos and logos), your employees should be willing to listen to what you have to say. Respect was a monumental factor to Steve Jobs’ success. With a strong engineering and developing background, Steve Jobs understood his employees and they in turn respected his opinions. One of the ways Jobs achieved this was by promoting staff that are experts in their field to managing the departments. Jobs didn’t like to hire people solely trained in managing teams. This led to high quality work from each individual department that when put together, resulted in perfect business practice. For example, the graphics department would choose photos for the online store, not the store’s manager. Jobs made sure that each executive kept their departments perfect, and didn’t involve themselves with anybody else’s area. This is one of the key pieces to how Apple works. It reduces bureaucracy, thus increasing productivity. Another bonus of this style of management, is it makes disciplining executives and managers easier. If one person is

responsible for the outcome of a department and easily replaceable by other employees in the same department then when the department doesn’t hit its targets or fails drastically, then the executive can be easily dismissed. This led to Steve Jobs not only being respected, but also feared, he wasn’t afraid of shouting at his executives, nor would he hesitate in firing them. When MobileMe flopped in 2008, the team responsible reportedly received a severe telling off and the executive in charge was quickly replaced. Using fear as a management technique is not recommended by business experts. It’s an extremely negative business strategy that is quite sure to make your employees unhappy. The only reason Jobs was able to use fear so effectively is because working for Apple was such a privilege, it is the most desirable job for electronics engineers and designers. Though following Jobs’ example and breaking rules to do what you think is best, this one is a risky maneuver. You may want to develop your business to the points of innovation and respect that Apple possessed before trying to instill fear into the hearts of your coworkers. Still, charisma, respect and innovation should lead your firmly along that path. Nonetheless, as an executive or CEO you should be present at every decision and have every serious choice run by you first. Your employees should be trying to impress you. Jobs imposed strict deadlines on every Apple department, again this utilizes a healthy level of fear. One great reason to work on Jobs like charisma, other than being able to be a feared presence in the office and get away with it, is the ability to motivate people. When properly motivated employees can reach new heights, taking your business further. Money works as a motivating factor, but this isn’t necessarily the Steve Jobs way. By inspiring your employees to innovate, and giving them space to grow,

every individual has the capability to explore new ideas and create groundbreaking products. Many businesses use some kind of reward system to generate more interest within mundane tasks. Though being truly passionate about your product, and employing people that believe in your company will inspire a motivated atmosphere in the workplace, great passion quickly becomes very contagious. A motivational speech here and there along with a keen eye on any developments will push your employees to work that little bit harder. Remember to congratulate and reward success. One of the simpler, yet most important things Steve Jobs did in Apple, was to only hire people passionate about the Apple brand. When your employees truly love and care about your product, they will go that extra mile for the company. Employees are more likely to enjoy the work, or at least be less phased by more grueling tasks if they believe in what they are doing. Hiring the right people will keep their morale up, as well as develop a nice community within the company.

Chapter 3 – Effective Marketing There was a time when Apple was not the leading force in consumer electronics that it is today. During the 1990s, Apple sold its products through numerous retailers and as a result, their gadgets became just another drop of water in a vast ocean of computers. The retailers lost respect for Apple products and then refused to properly market, or even stock Apple computers. Apple had to find a better way, and so they did. They began to ‘Think Different.’ Apple is famous for taking complex products – the PC, the MP3 player, downloadable music and the mobile phone – and making them simpler. The Mac may have had less functions than the pc, but it was more user-friendly. Common MP3s made users rip, copy, organize and transfer music files using various pieces of software, the iPod came with iTunes and made buying, downloading and transferring music extremely easy. The iPod automatically synced your music whilst it charged and it all it took was plugging in one cable. Apple wanted the public to know how simple it could be. Apple wanted you to have the easy life. “Marketing is about values. It’s a complicated and noisy world, and we’re not going to get a chance to get people to remember much about us. No company is. So we have to be really clear about what we want them to know about us.” – Steve Jobs. What Jobs did well, was standing out from the crowd. Simplicity and elegance became staple features in everything Apple produced. Their products were not just designed for geeks and wizards, they were for the everyman. Jobs replicated this in himself, by dressing in his own unique fashion, standing out from other CEOs. Marketers call this ‘establishing a rapport’, something Jobs did extremely well. The guys at Apple are brilliant at establishing rapport. Jobs famously dislikes

market research because, “A lot of times, people don’t know what they want until you show it to them.” When Jobs first opened Apple stores, they were originally laid out by product category, reflecting Apple’s internal structure as well as replicating a lot of what many other stores were doing at the time. Luckily for Jobs, he realized that this design would not bode well with their customers, and so the store was redesigned to reflect the products themselves – simple and sleek. This simple and sleek style made Apple stores extremely popular and strengthened the Apple brand image of being simple, yet different. If you think about it, all Apple products aren’t new designs, they’re simplified versions of existing products, with very clever marketing. Instead of selling a product, what Apple sell, is a lifestyle. I’m sure you can remember the television adverts? The ones in which a silhouette dances against a colorful and constantly changing background, fuelled by the distinctive white headphones and a little white box in the silhouettes hand? The interesting thing is that at no point are you shown the iPod’s interface, how it works, or any of its features. If you ask yourself why, the answer is simple. Apple aren’t selling the product, they’re selling the experience of owning an iPod. An MP3 player lets you listen to music, but an iPod makes you dance. What Steve Jobs did with marketing was create a new social class, an exclusive club of fun-loving people with an eye for style, and he did it well. He did it so well in fact, that people bought completely into Apple culture, becoming a fan of the brand and recommending its products to their friends. People didn’t just own one Apple product, they bought Macs, iPods, iPhones, iPads and used iTunes and the iCloud to bring it all together. The result? Each customer became a walking advert for Apple. The white headphones being the only part of an iPod constantly on show, they weren’t designed to be the best in

reproducing sound, they were a mark of being part of the Apple culture, of being in the club. Market your products as part of a culture, create a club that anyone can become a part of and feel good about themselves. Harley- Davidson effectively created an entire subculture based around their motorcycles, to the point people were getting Harley-Davidson tattoos. Their customers became walking, talking adverts. Develop a community around your product, market your product as a lifestyle instead of a thing, and create a memorable brand image that stands out from the crowd, you’ll bring customers in from all over the world and at minimal expense too.

Chapter 4 – Innovative thinking “Your time is limited, don’t waste it living someone else’s life. Don’t be trapped by dogma, which is living the result of other people’s thinking. Don’t let the noise of other opinions drown your own inner voice. And most important, have the courage to follow your heart and intuition, they somehow already know what you truly want to become. Everything else is secondary.” – Steve Jobs To design the best products that the public can get excited about, to create marketing strategies that draw people in and absorb them, to be the brand that people go to when they think of your field, you need to stand out from the crowd. Innovative ideas don’t come from following the same path over and over again. You have to experiment. Go off the beaten track. Steve Jobs believed that gathering as many personal experiences throughout one’s life is vital to create designs and arrive at ideas that no one else had conceived yet. Researchers at Harvard University studied the world’s greatest innovators for over half a decade. What they discovered about these ‘brilliant minds’ was not that they were geniuses, or vastly more intelligent, they discovered that innovators take ideas from other fields, experiences or aspects of life, and then apply it to the product or service that they are developing. Steve Jobs took a college course in calligraphy, at the time it appeared to bear no relevance to his life, but then when Macintosh was released, it became the first computer with attractive typefaces, fonts and calligraphy.

Experimentation Experimentation is a huge part of innovation. Jobs was famously quoted as saying that taking LSD, a powerful hallucinogen, was one of the most important events in his life. Jobs was at college, a time when young people traditionally experiment with recreational drugs and open themselves up to new experiences. The powerful psychedelic drug famously alters your perception and causes people to look at things from a different perspective. “LSD shows you that there’s﻿another side to the coin, and you can’t remember it when it wears off, but you know it.” – Steve Jobs. Of course going out and taking illegal drugs isn’t necessarily going to give you the idea for the next big thing, but that level of daringness, that experimental edge will give you fresh experiences to draw unique ideas from.

Breaking Rules Steve Jobs broke all the rules. His friends and colleagues have said that he had to, something within him would not let him conform. Every manufacturer of consumer electronics was adding more and more frivolous features to their products in the hopes that their gimmicks would win over the public. Apple went in the complete opposite direction, they stripped back user functions making their products easier and simpler to use. The lack of features did not mean the iPod had less thought or development, quite on the contrary, it took an incredible amount of coding to make the iPod as simple to use as it is. Let’s say your product is cars, imagine every automotive manufacturer is striving to produce the fastest, most powerful car ever conceived. Your engineers are struggling to keep up with the likes of Lamborghini, Ferrari, Aston Martin, and Porsche and so on. Instead you decide to not forget the trend. What you do, is spend all of your time and money engineering a luxurious interior, a smooth engine, you design it to be quiet and dignified. Your car becomes a symbol of class and status. You effectively stand out in all aspects other than what your competitors are doing. Non-conformity is crucial to innovation. By copying your competition and following the rules they lay out you’ll do nothing but drown amongst the million other middle of the road companies. Stand out and be brave. A great symbol of bravery is not being afraid to upset people. We’ve seen examples of Steve Jobs’ ruthlessness in the workplace, if someone’s work was not up to the standard required then Jobs would not be afraid to discipline them. You can’t take on every idea proposed within your business, it isn’t possible nor beneficial. You have to be able to simply say ‘no’. Steve Jobs once said, “Innovation

comes from saying no to 1,000 things.” When Jobs returned to Apple after a twelve year split he axed so many products that the remaining few had so many people dedicated to them, they reached far greater quality. Even today Apple only has a small number of products with a few variations of each. The less things you have to think about, the more you can perfect whatever feature it is that you are focusing on. Not everyone in the world will like your product, you need to focus on the people that will. You have to know your audience, and the best way to do this is create products for yourself. If you fall into your own audience, then the need for market research and focus groups is eliminated. Steve Jobs famously said at Apple they only made products for themselves. It goes back to what we mentioned earlier in business practices, only hire people who are passionate about your product, they’ll contribute the innovative ideas that will appeal to your audience. If you try to cater to everyone, you’ll end up not satisfying anyone. So to create groundbreaking products and innovative ideas like Steve Jobs, you have to gather as many personal experiences as possible and use them to inspire your work. You have to experiment, use your bravery to go where no one has gone before. Even if something doesn’t appear to work for you at first, you should still try it in case you are pleasantly surprised. And if experimentation didn’t work, you still have the experience to draw ideas from.

Chapter 5 – Mindset “I truly believe in positive synergy, that your positive mindset gives you a more hopeful outlook, and belief that you can do something great means you will do something great.” – Russell Wilson Maintaining a positive mindset is crucial to any good business leader. There will no doubt be times when you will be pushed onto your back foot. Throughout the 90s Apple was in a period of massive decline, poor sales and negative rifts developing within the company caused Steve Jobs to leave his role at Apple. When Jobs returned in 1997, he put the past behind them, maintained a positive outlook, cut Apple’s more frivolous products and restructured the entire company. Jobs swallowed his pride and reinvented the company he had co- founded many years before, into the sleek business that we all know and love today. If the employees and leaders of a company are enjoying themselves and having fun with the business, it is reflected onto all aspects of the company. This quickly becomes something that the customer associates with the company. For example, have you ever gone into a shop or restaurant in which all the employees are clearly miserable? The atmosphere is infectious and makes you want to leave the grim establishment as soon as possible, you don’t have to be told that is bad for business. We just mentioned Jobs’ return to Apple after being fired, we can learn a lot about mindset from this comeback. This is a perfect example of how beneficial swallowing one’s pride can be. Steve Jobs never quit Apple, he was forced to leave. Some might hold a grudge, but not Jobs. He came back and worked unbelievably hard. Pride never got in Jobs’ way, and neither did negativity, he remained positive and determined and that is the key to bringing Apple out of a

huge decline. If Jobs did not return to Apple, we cannot say what Apple would be doing in this day and age, but we can say that it would be very, very different. Jobs was fired by Apple’s board of directors for personal reasons, primarily because he was temperamental and difficult to control. Being fired for these reasons is quite the personal affront, and something that someone with those qualities wouldn’t take too lightly. Still, time helped Jobs mature and develop his leadership skills and charisma to the point that he would turn Apple around. Many of us, if fired from the company we co-founded were asked to return, would probably refuse and watch the company’s demise with glee. This is not good business practice. In fact, Jobs was not asked back to Apple, but instead worked his way back into the company. During Apple’s years of hardship, Jobs was running his new company NeXT. NeXT was working on revolutionary new software platform that was supposedly one of the best in the world. Apple had been having recent troubles with their developing OS. They found that it was becoming quickly outdated, and because of consistent delays, when it would be released, no one would want it. The CEO of Apple, Gil Amelio, scrapped the project and began looking for another OS to buy. An employee working for NeXT under Jobs supposedly told the Apple executives about what Jobs’ company had been working on and Apple became very interested. Soon after Steve Jobs turned up at Apple for the first time since his dismissal and not only convinced the Apple executives of buying the NeXT OS, but also of buying his entire company. Jobs was given 1.5 million Apple shares and appointed ‘informal advisor’ to Gil Amelio. It was not long before Amelio was removed and Jobs once more took his place as CEO of Apple. When Steve Jobs returned as CEO he made drastic changes to Apple’s internal structure. Within two years Jobs used the NeXT OS in Apple

computers and created the iMac, selling over 800,000 units within just five months. In five years the first Apple retail stores were opened and the iPod was released. 100 million iPods were sold over the next six years, proving that Jobs turned Apple from a falling star, into a force to be reckoned with. This was a period of major growth for Apple, and that’s what Steve Jobs wanted. Profit was not necessarily maximized but operations were set up to ensure that Apple would continually grow for the next few years and eventually demand great profits in the future. You too can achieve monumental goals, but you have to set them for yourself. They must be realistic and achievable but make sure you are aiming high. Failure to achieve your goals because you sought to monopolize an entire industry within one year may put a dent in your positive outlook, but realistically that is an incredibly difficult goal. Try to take risks, Jobs took a great risk by returning to Apple. NeXT were doing incredibly well financially, whilst Apple had been on a downward spiral for the last 7 years. It appeared Jobs had fled a sinking ship, and should have watched it go down smiling, but instead he bit the bullet and followed his intuition. Instead of fading into a distant memory, which Apple looked like it would, Jobs and NeXT revolutionized the company and put them back on the map in the consumer electronics world. Taking risks can be scary, you relinquish all control and put your success in the hands of fate, of course it’s scary. Still, you can’t go far without taking risks. Achieving great success doesn’t come down to just talent, you need a fair amount of luck. Play your cards right by following your intuition and it won’t even seem like gambling.

Conclusion If you follow these tips and learn from the great CEO that was Steve Jobs, your company will have a much greater chance of success. Remember you’ll need to be charismatic, talking to people and to the public is a huge part of being a brilliant CEO. Maintain friendly relationships with your workers and listen to what they have to say, be ever present and demand respect. Use the great management skills put forward by Steve Jobs. With respect and charisma you can take your employees much further than you otherwise would be able to. Apple was built on a ‘top-down’ structure, meaning that each executive of a department once worked in that department and was promoted for exceptional ability. This has numerous benefits: it keeps employee morale and respect because every worker knows that their superior has been through the same struggles as them and that perhaps one day, they can be an executive. This also makes holding executives accountable for department mistakes significantly easier, an executive will always ensure that only the best is coming from their department because if they are accountable and something goes wrong, they can quickly and easily be replaced by one of their staff. Marketing can be a great tool. Instead of going down the traditional route of advertising the new and great features of your product, try to develop a culture around your product. Sell a concept, not a commodity. If, like Apple or Harley-Davidson, you succeed in selling a lifestyle instead of a product, your customers and fans will advertise for you. Experiment with as many ideas as possible and try to have new experiences as much as you can. Draw from your personal experiences and use them to create new and innovative ideas. Be daring and try to

break the mold as often as possible. That is how to stop your ideas from becoming stale and cliché. Keep a positive mindset. If you get fired, go out and develop yourself until they beg for you back. If your company runs close to bankruptcy, make the change to set you back on the upward path. It’s like they say, ‘winners never quit, and quitters never win.’
